lessons.explanation: The loop's stopping rule is an iteration count, and that is the bug. Normal requests need 20 to 30 tool calls, so a cap of 10 cuts them off. The right rule is `stop_reason`: the loop continues while it is `tool_use` and finishes on `end_turn`, the normal finish. A cap stays only as a backstop for a run that goes wrong. The stem sets two requirements and the correct answer must meet both: protect against a runaway loop, and do not cut off normal work.

a.reasoning: The model signals when it has finished, so a run of 5 calls and a run of 30 calls both stop at the right moment. A cap of 60 sits well above the 20 to 30 calls normal work needs, so it never fires on healthy runs, yet it still catches the infinite-loop bug that caused the cap to be added. Both requirements in the stem are met.

b.reasoning: It fails both requirements in different ways. The text check can fire early, because the model can write that phrase in a status update while it still has tool calls to make. Dropping the cap removes the runaway-loop protection the stem says to keep. The text check also adds nothing, because `end_turn` already says the model is done.
b.tempting: It starts with `stop_reason`, which is right, and dropping the cap looks like the cure for the 18% of cut-off runs.

c.reasoning: It keeps the cap of 10, so the 18% of runs that need 20 to 30 calls would still be cut off, which fails the requirement not to cut off normal work. The stall rule adds a second problem: useful iterations such as a dataset lookup or a check of a figure add no new documents, so three in a row would end a healthy run. It is also homemade logic layered on a signal the API already gives.
c.tempting: It starts with `stop_reason` and calls the cap a safety net, which is the correct idea. The cap's number is what gives it away.

d.reasoning: The count is still the stopping rule, only bigger. A run that finishes after 5 calls keeps going to 40, and the first request that needs 45 calls is cut off again. Reading `stop_reason` only to log it throws away the signal that should decide when to stop.
d.tempting: A cap of 40 sits above the longest runs seen so far, so it looks safe. It is tuned to the past, not to the model's signal.

concept: An agentic loop sends the request and reads `stop_reason`. While it is `tool_use`, the loop runs the requested tools, appends the results to the conversation and sends again. `end_turn` is the normal finish, so the loop returns. The documented loop keeps calling the API while `stop_reason` is `tool_use` and returns otherwise.

Other stop reasons exist, such as `max_tokens` (output truncated), `pause_turn`, `refusal` and `model_context_window_exceeded`, so a response that is not `tool_use` is not always a clean finish and the others need their own handling. Agents commonly have a maximum number of iterations to keep control, which supports a cap as a safety net. The exam guide's anti-patterns are an iteration cap as the primary stopping rule, parsing natural language to end the loop and checking the assistant's text for completion.

lessons.explanation: Citations are lost when the findings are handed to the synthesis subagent, for two reasons. The handover is unstructured, so URLs and page numbers sit in prose and the subagent has to dig them out. And the subagent sees only the prompt it is given, so anything missing from that prompt does not exist for it. The fix has two halves: put the complete findings in the prompt, and pass them in a form where each claim's source is its own field.

a.reasoning: The subagent would redo work the other subagents already did, guessing which documents a sentence came from using only the prose it was given. It is slower and less reliable than carrying the source forward with each claim from the start.
a.tempting: It sounds like a cheap way to add citations, but it repairs the gap after the draft is written instead of at the handover.

b.reasoning: When each claim carries its own source URL, document title and page number as separate fields, citing becomes copying instead of digging through prose. This fixes how the source is carried, and it is one half of the fix.

c.reasoning: It hides the gap instead of closing it: about 15% of the claims would be deleted, not cited. The second pass has no more source data than the first, so it cannot add citations. Provenance has to travel with the findings.
c.tempting: It makes the output look compliant, and the word 'removes' is easy to read past.

d.reasoning: A subagent does not see the coordinator's conversation or the other subagents' work, so the complete findings have to be in its own prompt. This is the other half of the fix: one change says how to pass the findings, this one says what to pass and where.
d.tempting: The stem says the findings are already pasted, so this can look like a no-op. But paragraphs of prose are a summary that has already lost detail.

e.reasoning: The subagent starts fresh, so there is no earlier discussion for it to read. Pointing it at sources it never received makes things worse: it would leave citations out or invent them.
e.tempting: In one conversation with one model, a phrase like 'discussed above' works. The trap is carrying that habit over to subagents.

concept: A subagent started through the `Task` tool begins fresh: it does not see the parent's conversation, tool results or other subagents' output. The only thing the parent passes is the prompt string, so findings, file paths and decisions must be written into it. There is no shared memory, and only the subagent's final message comes back to the parent. Since Claude Code v2.1.63 the tool is named `Agent`; `Task` still works as an alias and is the name the exam uses.

When the subagent must cite its sources, how you pass the data matters as much as what you pass. Use a structured format that keeps content (the claim, the excerpt) separate from metadata (URL, title, page number), so the source cannot be lost between handoffs. Anthropic's research system also adds a separate citation step after synthesis; that is background here, not a fix for this stem.

lessons.rule: A subagent knows only its prompt. Put the complete findings in it, with each claim's source in its own field.

lessons.explanation: The fixed plan decided in advance what to read, based on an assumption about how the code is laid out, and the assumption was wrong. Nothing found along the way could change the plan. This is an open-ended investigation: you do not know where the answer is. So the plan should come from looking at the codebase and change as findings arrive. The two fixes work together: map the structure first, then plan from that map and keep revising.

a.reasoning: A quick map with `Glob` and `Grep` shows the Python scoring module before 60 Java files are read. Starting from structure replaces the assumption in the fixed plan with what is actually in the codebase. It is one half of the fix.

b.reasoning: It adds one more fixed step and places it late, so the agent reads the Java callees first and reaches the scoring module last. The plan is still fixed in advance, so the next codebase will have another blind spot.
b.tempting: It patches exactly the gap the stem shows, which makes it look like the targeted fix.

c.reasoning: An adaptive plan lets what is found steer the next step, for example moving to the scoring module once the time is seen to go there. Together with the map it focuses effort on the high-impact areas, which a one-hour deadline needs.

d.reasoning: The problem is choosing what to read, not reading fast enough. Reading all 1.4 million lines in parallel is brute force, and merged notes from every directory bury the one module that matters. Parallel work suits independent pieces, not an investigation that follows clues.
d.tempting: The stem has a deadline, and parallel work sounds like speed. It never decides where to look, so it does not fix why the plan failed.

e.reasoning: General encouragement does not change the order of a fixed plan or tell the agent where to look first, so it would run exactly as before. Being exhaustive is also the wrong goal under a one-hour deadline.
e.tempting: It names the real blind spot, the other language, without changing how the plan is made.

concept: There are two ways to split a task into steps. Prompt chaining is a fixed sequence decided up front, which suits predictable work where you know every step, such as a pass over each file followed by a cross-file pass. Dynamic decomposition creates the next subtasks from what the last step found, which suits open-ended problems where the number of steps cannot be predicted or hard-coded.

For open-ended work the guide's pattern is: map the structure, find the high-impact areas, then make a prioritised plan that adapts as you learn. An agent has to observe its environment and adjust its approach from what it sees, and research agents do better starting with short, broad queries to see what is available, then narrowing. Performance hunts and 'why does it take so long' questions are open-ended.

lessons.rule: When you do not know where the answer is, map the structure first, rank by impact, and let each finding change the plan.

lessons.explanation: The four checks are known in advance and are the same on every pull request, in the same order. Letting Claude plan the review caused both symptoms: plans vary, so some runs skip the changelog, and the planning step adds cost a fixed chain doesn't have, with the adaptive review costing three times as much as the old script. Both come from planning a task that needs no planning. The fix removes the planning decision and runs a fixed prompt chain. This is the mirror image of an open-ended investigation, where a fixed plan fails.

a.reasoning: A fixed chain of four prompts gives every pull request exactly the four checks in order, so the changelog can never be skipped. No planning step runs, so its cost goes away. When the steps are known, a chain is predictable in both coverage and cost.

b.reasoning: A prompt instruction only nudges a planner whose output already varies, so some runs would still skip a check, and the planning step keeps adding cost a fixed chain doesn't have. A fixed chain removes the decision instead of asking the model to make it correctly.
b.tempting: Listing the four checks by name sounds like it closes the gap, but it is still an instruction to a variable planner.

c.reasoning: The chain is the right base, but letting the model add steps whenever it decides brings a planning decision back, with the extra cost the stem complains about, for a list of checks that never changes. Nothing in the stem asks for more checks.
c.tempting: It sounds like the best of both: a reliable chain plus flexibility. It adds a feature the stem never asked for, and that feature brings back the planning cost.

d.reasoning: Running small PRs' plans on a smaller model adds a layer that makes the planning cheaper but leaves it variable. Having the agent list its planned checks first is still the agent's own plan, so a run can leave out the changelog. The gap comes from planning a task that never changes, and the planning step adds cost a fixed chain doesn't have.
d.tempting: It attacks the cost complaint directly, but it adds a routing layer and keeps the planning.

concept: Ask one question first: do I know the steps before I start? If yes, such as the same checks in the same order every time, use a fixed prompt chain. Each call processes the previous output, with optional programmatic checks between steps, and Claude does better on one focused task than on many requirements at once. A chain is accurate, predictable and easy to test.

If no, such as debugging or exploring unknown code, use dynamic decomposition: the steps come from what each step finds. Agents are more flexible but have a lower completion rate and are harder to test, and the best advice is to start with the simplest solution and add complexity only when it clearly improves results. Using adaptive planning for fixed work adds cost and variation.

stemSignals.meaning: The adaptive review costs more, and part of that is the planning step a fixed chain doesn't have. The fix should remove planning, not make it cheaper.

No step where the model decides what the review should contain.

It lets the model add steps, which puts the planning decision back in for a list that never changes.
It makes planning cheaper but keeps it, so the changelog can still be skipped.

lessons.rule: Known steps call for a fixed chain; an unknown path calls for mapping and adapting. Do not add flexibility a fixed task does not need.

lessons.explanation: The ban comes from a regulator, and the stem shows prompt text has already stopped helping: a third example and a bold warning cut the monthly count only from 3 to 2. Compliance wants zero. A rule that must always hold needs enforcement in code at a fixed point in the loop, before the call runs. A hook that runs before the notice tool and checks the flag blocks the call, sends the agent to the human path, and adds nothing to the 99% of notices that are allowed.

a.reasoning: Examples are a probabilistic nudge, and the stem shows they have already stopped working. A regulatory ban needs a guarantee, so more prompt text is the wrong layer. Examples suit gray-area judgment, not a legal prohibition.
a.tempting: Examples worked a little (3 to 2), so more of them feels like the natural next step.

b.reasoning: A hook that runs after the tool has already fired is too late: the notice has gone out and the rule is already broken. Voiding and alerting only report the breach. Blocking has to happen before the call.
b.tempting: It has the right trigger, the flag from the account lookup, and a good clean-up story. It runs at the wrong point.

c.reasoning: A hook that runs before the tool intercepts the call, so no notice can reach a register customer, and the block message sends the agent to the approved human path. The check is deterministic code, so it guarantees the rule, and the allowed notices are not slowed.

d.reasoning: The register flag is already available from the account lookup, so a predictive classifier adds a new component with its own error rate to settle something the data already settles. A classifier is worth it only when no explicit field exists.
d.tempting: A dedicated check sounds thorough, but it replaces a certain field with a guess.

concept: An instruction in a prompt or in CLAUDE.md is a request, not a guarantee: Claude usually follows it, but prompts alone have a non-zero failure rate. A hook is deterministic code that runs at a fixed point in the loop, so it can guarantee a behaviour. The exam guide favours hooks and gates over prompt instructions for rules that must always hold.

`PreToolUse` fires before a tool call and is the enforcement primitive: it can return a decision to deny the call, with a reason that Claude sees, and exit code 2 also blocks. `PostToolUse` fires after the tool already ran, so blocking there cannot stop the call or its side effects.

lessons.explanation: The approvers lose 8 minutes because the handoff says only that a credit needs approval. A good handoff compresses the case into structured facts for the next person: who the customer is, what is disputed, the root cause and the recommended action. The two answers that fit are the identifiers with the proposed amount, and the root cause with its supporting evidence. Together they say which case this is and why the credit is justified, in a few lines.

a.reasoning: Dumping the whole session recreates the 8-minute reading task the approvers already complain about. A handoff should compress the case into the few facts needed to decide. A transcript can be an attachment but cannot replace a summary.
a.tempting: It is complete, so nothing is missing, but completeness is exactly what the approvers are drowning in.

b.reasoning: These are the facts the approver is currently hunting for in the chat: the verified account, the disputed bill and the proposed credit. With them in the handoff the approver can open the right records straight away.

c.reasoning: A score gives the approver a number to trust without a reason, and it leaves out the account and bill details the approver needs. A decision should rest on stated evidence, not on how sure the model says it is.
c.tempting: A single number is short, which fits the need for a quick read.

d.reasoning: This is the same kind of generic message the approvers already complain about: it says nothing about the account, the cause or the amount, so the approver still has to dig for every fact. Urgency is not a substitute for case facts.

e.reasoning: The cause and its evidence tell the approver why a credit is justified without re-reading the chat. It complements the identifiers: one says which case this is, the other says why the proposed credit is right.

concept: When work passes from the agent to a person, the handoff should be a structured summary, not a raw dump or a one-line flag. The exam guide's examples of what it carries are the customer identifier, the root cause and the recommended actions.

Structure is what keeps it short enough to read at a glance: each field answers one question the next person would otherwise have to hunt for. In a 'select 2' question, write down each problem first and match one answer to each.

lessons.explanation: The agent resolves the first two items and forgets the third in 30% of multi-issue messages, while single-issue conversations are fine. That is a planning and attention problem, not a compliance rule: no money or regulation is at stake, and the team wants no new components. The exam guide's approach is to split a multi-concern request into distinct items, investigate each, and give one resolution. A line in the system prompt asking for exactly that is the smallest fix that targets the cause.

a.reasoning: Multi-issue messages are within the agent's reach, and the resolution target depends on handling them. Escalating all of them is premature and throws away what the agent can resolve. Escalation is for explicit human requests or policy gaps, not for message length.
a.tempting: Handing off feels safe, but it trades a 30% miss for a human on every multi-issue message.

b.reasoning: This builds enforcement machinery for a planning problem. The agent never sees the missing item, so a counter would block the reply without telling it what is missing. Neither money nor regulation is at stake, so code-level enforcement is not needed.
b.tempting: A counter sounds like a guarantee, and hooks are the usual answer to misses. Here nothing must be enforced.

c.reasoning: This pushes the problem onto the customer and leaves the agent's weakness untouched. It also lowers the resolution rate, because customers will drop the extra items.
c.tempting: It would make the agent's job easier, but it changes the customer's behaviour instead of fixing the agent.

d.reasoning: Listing each distinct request, investigating each one and covering every item in a single reply gives each item its own investigation and makes a missing item visible when the reply is composed. This is a judgment and planning problem with nothing to enforce, so guidance in the system prompt is the smallest right fix.

concept: Pick the layer by what the problem needs. When compliance must be guaranteed, such as money or regulation, use a hook or gate, because a prompt has a non-zero failure rate. When the need is judgment and nothing must be enforced, guidance in the system prompt is the right and simplest tool. Start with the simplest solution and add complexity only when it clearly improves results.
For a request that holds several concerns, the exam guide's skill is to split it into distinct items, investigate each, and give one resolution.

lessons.explanation: The two meter tools return different units and different status formats, and a prompt table has only cut the error rate from 11% to 8%. The reliable fix is a hook that runs after each tool call and rewrites what the model sees, so the model only ever reasons about one unit and plain-language statuses. Normalising both the unit and the status codes in code leaves nothing for the model to get wrong.

a.reasoning: The stem shows the prompt table was already tried and left an 8% error rate. More examples and a self-check keep the work probabilistic, so the result still depends on the model getting each conversion right.
a.tempting: It builds on what already helped a little, and a double-check sounds careful.

b.reasoning: A hook before the call acts on the outgoing arguments, but the mismatch is in what the tools send back. Rewriting arguments cannot change the numeric reading type or the unit the legacy tool returns. Normalisation belongs in the result path, after the call.
b.tempting: It also normalises something with a hook, but it runs on the wrong side of the call.

c.reasoning: A hook after the call can replace the tool result the model sees, so the model gets one unit and readable statuses from both tools. It is deterministic code, unlike the prompt table, which cut errors from 11% to only 8%.

d.reasoning: Converting only the units fixes half of the mismatch. The numeric reading types still depend on a prompt legend, which is where the model keeps calling bills estimated by mistake. Normalising both fields in code is what removes the error.
d.tempting: It uses the right hook, and it is close. The leftover legend in the prompt is the gap.

concept: `PostToolUse` fires after the tool ran and can replace what the model sees with `updatedToolOutput`, and it can add context with `additionalContext`. That makes it the place to normalise heterogeneous formats, such as Unix timestamps, ISO 8601 dates and numeric status codes, before the model processes them. Hooks are deterministic and prompts are probabilistic.

`PreToolUse` acts on the outgoing call instead: it can allow, deny or rewrite the input with `updatedInput`. Choose the hook point by where the problem is: arguments going out, or results coming back.
